title: Hormone messages: the control room
subtitle: Trace a chemical message and explain a controlled response
objective: Describe endocrine signalling and explain why suitable internal conditions matter.

sow.alignment: Directly develops C30 through Pearson7.1,7.9 and selected7.10B concepts. Core names endocrine glands and blood transport, with pancreas/insulin as a simple example. Detailed adrenaline, thyroxine feedback and reproductive hormone mechanisms are not claimed as covered.

priorLearning: Blood transports substances around the body.
Cells carry out reactions using enzymes.
External conditions can change while an organism remains alive.
success: Explain why a circulating hormone does not affect every cell equally.
Explain homeostasis as regulation within suitable limits rather than perfect stillness.

vocabulary.meaning: A chemical messenger released by an endocrine gland and carried in blood.
An organ or tissue that releases hormones into the bloodstream.
A cell able to respond to a particular hormone, usually because it has the appropriate receptor.
A molecule that recognises a signal and can trigger a response.
Regulation of internal conditions within suitable limits despite change.
A response that reduces the original departure from a regulated condition.

equipment: Shared evidence sheet, one selected response route, pen and ruler.
Projector or offline HTML/PowerPoint; calculator where useful.
preparation: Print the shared page, one selected response route and the exit page. Routes are alternatives, not extra tasks.
Read the worked answers and note any constructed data before teaching.
safety: Paper and screen lesson; no human sampling, exercise test, breath holding, medicine handling or personal health disclosure.
practicalAlternative: All evidence is supplied. Use paper diagrams and cards, pointing, annotation or dictation if a device is unavailable.

misconceptions.claim: A hormone travels only through a private tube to one organ.
misconceptions.correction: It circulates in blood; target cells respond because they can recognise the signal.
misconceptions.check: Ask why a nearby non-target cell may not respond.

misconceptions.claim: Every cell responds identically to every hormone.
misconceptions.correction: Cells differ in receptors and response machinery.

misconceptions.claim: Homeostasis means a condition never changes.
misconceptions.correction: Regulation limits departures; suitable ranges and dynamic adjustment matter.
misconceptions.check: Ask whether a small change automatically means control has failed.

misconceptions.claim: All homeostatic responses must use hormones.
misconceptions.correction: Homeostasis can involve nervous and hormonal coordination.
misconceptions.check: Distinguish the general control idea from the endocrine example.

access.supported: Same core concepts with chunked prompts and read-aloud access. Record support used; a pathway is not a diagnosis or fixed attainment label.
access.standard: Explain the supplied evidence independently using accurate scientific terms and units.
access.stretch: Optional deeper transfer or evaluation. Higher-tier-only material is labelled explicitly and is not required for the core outcome.
access.regulation: Offer solo or partner work, a quiet response, a pass and brief reset with clear re-entry. No forced disclosure or public performance.

slides.title: How does a cell receive the right message?
body: A hormone can travel around the body in blood.
Why does every cell not react in the same way?
slides.notes: Invite a prediction without calling hormones thinking agents. Preview signal route, recognition and control.

slides.title: Transport and conditions
body: R1. What carries many dissolved substances around the body?
R2. Why do cells need suitable conditions?
R3. Does a chemical messenger think or choose?
slides.notes: R1: blood. R2: cell reactions/enzymes work effectively under suitable conditions. R3: no; interactions are physical/chemical. Accept plain-language mechanisms.

slides.title: I trace the message route
body: Gland releases → blood carries → target responds.
The hormone is a chemical messenger.
slides.notes: Model pancreas releasing insulin into blood; responsive tissues change glucose uptake/storage processes. Keep this preview qualitative. Endocrine secretion is into blood, not an exocrine duct.

visual.title: One message, three important locations
visual.description: Endocrine transport model: an endocrine gland releases a hormone into circulating blood; the hormone reaches tissues, but only appropriate target cells respond. Arrows show information/material transport, not a private gland-to-organ duct.

slides.title: Recognition makes the signal specific
body: Blood can bring a signal near many cells.
A target cell can recognise it and respond.
slides.notes: Think aloud: “Both cells are exposed, so travel alone cannot explain the difference. Cell A has the appropriate receptor. The simplified shape represents molecular recognition, not a key operated by a tiny person.”

visual.title: A circulating hormone needs a matching response
visual.description: Simplified receptor model: a purple signal is present near two cells. Cell A has a matching receptor and can respond; cell B lacks that receptor. Shapes model recognition only; real receptors are molecules, not conscious locks.

slides.title: Homeostasis keeps conditions suitable
body: Conditions change; regulation limits departures.
A corrective response reduces the original change.
Some control uses nerves, some uses hormones.
slides.notes: Model a raised internal variable and a response tending to lower it. Do not use universal numeric normal ranges. Link suitable temperature to enzyme activity and water balance to cell volume at a conceptual level.

visual.title: Control reduces a departure
visual.description: General negative-feedback model: a condition departs from a suitable range, the change is detected/coordinated, a response opposes the departure, and the condition moves towards the range. This is a control concept, not a claim that all responses are hormonal.

slides.title: Message-routing desk
body: W1. Locate the gland names using the position clues.
Then trace a pancreas hormone from release to response.
slides.notes: Use table. All six locations are curriculum gland knowledge; reproductive organs are named matter-of-factly without requiring personal information. Route pancreas→blood→appropriate target tissue.

table.caption: Schematic location guide; different reproductive organs are listed, not drawn as one anatomy.

slides.title: Predict the responding cell
body: W2. The same hormone reaches cells A and B.
Which cell is more likely to respond in this model?
slides.notes: A has matching receptor. Ask for the missing link if pupil says hormone never reaches B; it does reachB but no matching response is represented.

slides.title: Control-room repair
body: W3. “The variable rose, so the controller always pushes it further up.”
Explain what a negative-feedback response should do.
slides.notes: It counteracts the original rise, tending towards suitable limits. Do not claim every biological loop is negative feedback or control is instantaneous.
slides.reveal: A negative-feedback response opposes the departure, rather than automatically amplifying it.

slides.title: Which explanation links route and recognition?
body: Choose the mechanism, not a human-like story.
slides.notes: First option correct. Re-teach blood distribution versus recognition if wrong.

options.text: The hormone circulates; appropriate target cells recognise it and respond.
options.feedback: Yes. Transport and recognition are different parts of the mechanism.

options.text: The hormone chooses only the cells it likes.
options.feedback: Hormones do not choose; molecular recognition and cell machinery determine responses.

options.text: Homeostasis means no internal value ever changes.
options.feedback: Regulation responds to changes and helps keep conditions within suitable limits.

slides.title: Build a control explanation
body: Choose your response page.
Use a route diagram and a cause-and-effect sentence.
slides.notes: All routes target message transport, specificity and regulated conditions. No numerical clinical data are required.

slides.title: Make the mechanism visible
body: Source → transport → target → response.
Explain why suitable conditions matter.
slides.notes: Supported S1–S4; standard M1–M4; stretch T1–T4. Use a word-bank prompt if needed and record support. Do not require advanced hormone feedback cascades.

slides.title: Audience asks about the missing link
body: L1. Share a short explanation.
Audience: “How did the message reach that cell, and why did it respond?”
slides.notes: A quiet teacher/TA review counts. Pupil improves a route label or distinguishes exposure from response.

slides.title: A useful model also has a limit
body: The model shows a mechanism.
It does not predict exact timings, hormone amounts or clinical outcomes.
slides.notes: Model a precise limit. Keep homeostasis as dynamic regulation; avoid perfect thermostat equivalence.

slides.title: Three linked ideas
body: E1. How are endocrine hormones transported?
E2. Why may a non-target cell not respond?
E3. What does homeostasis regulate?
slides.notes: E1: in blood. E2: appropriate recognition/receptor absent in the model. E3: internal conditions within suitable limits. Use these to prepare the glucose model.

slides.title: Choose the next useful step
body: Gland location • signal route • target recognition • control.
slides.notes: Shared exit minute. Accept a labelled arrow chain instead of extended writing.

pupilPages.intro: Original conceptual cases; no personal health or medical decision is involved.

cards.title: Cell model
cards.text: A hormone is present near both cells A and B. A has a matching receptor; B lacks that receptor.

cards.title: Control case
cards.text: An internal variable rises above its usual suitable range. In this model, the control response can reduce that departure.

cards.title: Conditions case
cards.text: A cell’s enzyme-controlled reactions depend on suitable temperature. Water balance also affects animal-cell volume.

blocks.prompt: W1. Trace a message. W2. Predict a responding cell. W3. Explain a corrective response.

pupilPages.title: Supported route | Label the mechanism
pupilPages.intro: Word bank: endocrine gland; blood; target; receptor; response; suitable range.

blocks.prompt: S1. Put gland, blood and target cell in order. Say what happens at each step.
S2. Choose A or B from the cell model and explain the recognition difference.
S3. An internal variable rises. Describe the direction of a response that counteracts this rise.
S4. Give one reason suitable internal conditions matter. Locate the pancreas and thyroid.

pupilPages.title: Standard route | Explain the control room
pupilPages.intro: Use the shared evidence and accurate biological terms.

blocks.prompt: M1. Explain how a hormone reaches a target organ, distinguishing release, transport and response.
M2. Explain why cell A can respond when cell B does not, although both are exposed.
M3. Explain homeostasis and negative feedback without claiming perfect constancy or that all responses use hormones.
M4. Name the positions of three endocrine glands and explain one reason internal temperature or water balance matters.

pupilPages.title: Stretch route | Test the model
pupilPages.intro: Optional deeper reasoning; detailed Higher-tier hormone cascades are not required.

blocks.prompt: T1. A cell has a matching receptor but its response machinery is damaged. Is receptor presence alone enough to guarantee a normal response? Explain.
T2. A model response arrives late and the variable briefly passes its target. Does this prove there is no control? Explain one model limitation.
T3. Compare a broadly circulating chemical message with a directed nerve signal at a conceptual level. Avoid claiming all hormone responses are always slow.
T4. Explain why a general feedback diagram cannot predict a person’s exact hormone level or diagnose illness.

pupilPages.title: Exit and reflection | Route, recognition, regulation
pupilPages.intro: Use short explanations or labelled arrows.

blocks.prompt: E1. How do endocrine hormones travel to tissues?
E2. Why may a cell fail to respond to a particular hormone?
E3. What does homeostasis regulate, and why?
L1. What did your audience ask? Record one improved or defended mechanism.

answers.label: Retrieval and We do
answers.answer: R1: blood; R2: suitable conditions support cell reactions/enzymes and cell integrity; R3: no. W1: use the six locations in the table, then pancreas→blood→responsive tissue. W2: A has matching recognition. W3: the response should reduce the original rise in the model.

answers.label: Hinge
answers.answer: Correct: circulation plus target recognition. Hormones do not consciously choose. Homeostasis permits change while regulating within suitable limits.

answers.label: S1 / M1
answers.answer: An endocrine gland releases a hormone into blood. Circulating blood transports it to tissues. Cells with suitable recognition/response machinery respond by changing activity.

answers.label: S2 / M2
answers.answer: A has the matching receptor; B does not in this model. Both can encounter the hormone. Presence in blood is not the same as an appropriate target response.

answers.label: S3 / M3
answers.answer: A corrective response opposes the rise and tends towards suitable limits. Homeostasis regulates an internal environment; it does not mean every value is fixed or that all coordination is hormonal.

answers.label: S4 / M4
answers.answer: Pancreas upper abdomen; thyroid neck. Other valid locations: pituitary base of brain; adrenals above kidneys; ovaries pelvis; testes scrotum. Suitable temperature supports enzyme-controlled reactions; water balance prevents excessive cell swelling/shrinking.

answers.label: T1
answers.answer: No. Recognition is one requirement; downstream cell machinery must also function. The simple receptor picture omits those steps.

answers.label: T2
answers.answer: No. Delays and overshoot can occur in regulated systems. A simplified diagram does not show response speeds, competing signals or exact ranges.

answers.label: T3
answers.answer: Hormones circulate chemically in blood and affect responsive targets. Nerve impulses travel along neurones to connected targets. Typical timing/range differ, but avoid absolute claims that every hormone is slow or every response identical.

answers.label: T4
answers.answer: The model has no individual measurements, calibrated parameters or clinical context. It illustrates a causal organisation, not a diagnostic instrument.

answers.label: Exit and assessment
answers.answer: E1: bloodstream. E2: lack of appropriate receptor/response machinery; use the receptor distinction for core. E3: internal conditions within suitable limits so cells function. Secure core: correct route+specificity+dynamic regulation. Re-teach by separately asking “does the signal arrive?” and “can the cell respond?”

teacherNotes: 40-minute lesson. Zero-minute slides share the preceding stage allocation.
Choose one response route. Accept accurate speech, pointing with explanation, annotations or writing; record the support used.
A teacher or TA can be a quiet audience: ask one evidence question, then let the pupil revise or justify a decision.
Interactive We do uses the same gland-route, target-recognition and feedback cases. Pupils predict, reveal a mechanism and explain; paper W1–W3 follows the same decisions.
Naming ovaries and testes is part of locating endocrine structures; no pupil anatomy, identity, family history or health disclosure is required.
